home.identity: I am a Visiting Scholar at Harvard University, working with Yilun Du and Mengyu Wang on 4D world models for robotic planning. I am in the fourth year of my Ph.D. at the University of Hong Kong, under the supervision of Xiaojuan Qi. I have been awarded the Hong Kong PhD Fellowship (HKPFS) and the HKU Presidential Scholarship (HKUPS). Previously, I received dual B.S. degrees in Computer Engineering from Zhejiang University and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

home.research_statement: I am interested in world models for generalizable robotic planning: how robots can understand the physical world and use imagined futures to act in unfamiliar environments. My work makes geometry and motion explicit in these futures, connects them to robot actions, and develops the perception and memory needed to recover and retain useful evidence across observations. Looking ahead, I aim to explore agent–world model co-evolution, where interaction improves the world model, and the improved model supports better planning and policy learning.

research.question: What should a robot perceive, remember, and predict to act reliably in an unfamiliar environment?

directions.title: 4D world models for action
directions.text: I develop models that generate visual futures together with corresponding robot actions. Making geometry and motion explicit lets the predicted future guide action generation and support consistency checks before execution.
directions.source: S4NDBOX abstract and introduction; current CV02. Future-before-action modeling, not an already action-conditioned simulator or safety guarantee.

directions.title: Memory across views and time
directions.text: I study how models retain useful information as viewpoints change and sequences grow longer. Geometric working memory supports multi-view spatial reasoning, while recurrent state-space memory carries temporal context through long-video generation.
directions.source: Current CV02 and existing GaMe/VideoSSM project descriptions. These are distinct working-memory and generation methods, not an already unified persistent world model.

directions.title: Perception in changing environments
directions.text: I develop methods for recovering scene geometry and keeping dense predictions up to date when lighting is difficult or RGB observations are sparse. Event measurements provide complementary evidence as the scene changes.
directions.source: Current CV02 and existing EAG3R/LiFR project summaries. These works provide perceptual foundations; they are not all robot policies.

research.presentation_note: Reference for organization only: a central research question, short explanations, and concrete linked examples before publications. No text, research claims, taxonomy, or assets copied from the reference website.

about.background: I am a Visiting Scholar at Harvard University and a fourth-year Ph.D. student at the University of Hong Kong. I received dual B.S. degrees in Computer Engineering from Zhejiang University and UIUC through the ZJUI Institute.
perspective: I am interested in how robots can use a coherent understanding of the physical world to act reliably in unfamiliar environments. This requires more than recognizing what is in an image: a robot must recover spatial relationships, retain useful evidence across observations, and anticipate how the world may change.

My work approaches this question through spatial perception, geometric memory, and future prediction. The common goal is to make information about the world useful for action—not simply to produce another image or representation.
about.inspiration: Joi in <cite>Blade Runner 2049</cite> inspires my interest in AI as a presence in everyday life. For me, the research question is how to ground that presence in an understanding of the world, meaningful action, and the ability to learn from experience.
